Vignette: Mere

Mere is a 75-year-old Fijian woman who has been married to her husband Sione for fifty-one years. Until her retirement two years ago, she spent her career as a senior auditor for a regional development organization, a role that required precision, steadiness, and an almost architectural trust in order. She was known among colleagues as someone who could hold an entire financial landscape in her mind and find the single number that didn't belong. She prided herself on that clarity. It is the loss of that clarity, more than anything else, that she grieves now.

In 1987, Mere was living in Suva when Fiji's first military coup fractured the country she had always understood as peaceable. She was thirty-seven years old, pregnant with her third child, and working late at her office when soldiers moved through the commercial district. What began as a distant rumble of vehicles became, within hours, a neighborhood locked down by armed men she did not recognize as her countrymen. She was held for nearly eleven hours in her office building alongside four colleagues, unable to leave, unable to reach Sione or her children at home. At one point, soldiers entered the building and moved through the corridors. She heard shouting, the sound of something heavy being overturned, a single gunshot somewhere above her. She pressed herself against the wall behind a filing cabinet and did not move. She believed, with complete certainty, that she was going to die before her baby was born.

She did not die. The soldiers passed. By morning she was released and walked home through streets that looked almost normal, which felt more disturbing than the chaos had. Her daughter was born healthy three months later. Mere told almost no one what had happened. There was a country to rebuild, a family to raise, and work to return to. She filed it away the way she filed everything — neatly, out of sight.

For nearly three decades, the filing held. Then, in her early seventies, the structure began to give way. She is not entirely sure what loosened it. Perhaps retirement removed the scaffolding of routine that had kept everything in place. Perhaps it was the news — coups elsewhere, footage of soldiers in streets, sounds from a television in the next room that her brain could not distinguish from memory. She began waking at two or three in the morning, heart hammering, certain that someone was in the house. She would lie rigid beside Sione, listening, unable to convince herself that the sounds were ordinary. Some nights she smells something she cannot name — something metallic and close — that she knows is not really there.

During the day she avoids the evening news entirely. She has stopped attending her church's social gatherings because the noise of a crowd, the unpredictability of bodies moving around her, makes her feel as though the floor is tilting. At the supermarket last month, a security guard in a dark uniform walked past her and she abandoned her trolley and left the building without understanding why until she was sitting in her car, shaking. She told Sione she had felt unwell.

She has not told Sione what she experienced in that office building in 1987. She has never told him. She worries that doing so now, after fifty-one years of marriage, would mean explaining why she kept it from him, and she does not have language for that yet. Instead she finds herself short-tempered in ways that shame her, distant in ways that confuse him. She watches him sometimes across the dinner table and feels a tenderness so acute it frightens her, as though she is still that woman behind the filing cabinet calculating what she stands to lose.

She came to therapy, she says, because she could no longer audit her own mind. The numbers, as she puts it, no longer add up, and for the first time in her life, she does not know where to look for the error.
